doc.title: Tony Marino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 25, 2025

title: Playing with Al Cohn and Zoot Sims; young players and tunes
summary: Phil Woods's circle, first New York gig with Al Cohn at Fat Tuesday's, Zoot Sims at the Blue Note complaining about tunes, and Marino's dance-gig repertoire and fusion-era listening.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: This will be totally speculative, but you’ve played with some marvelous saxophone players over the years and I’m thinking in my mind comparing like Zoot Sims with Dave Liebman. Zoot Sims probably came early in your career.

Yeah. Well I used to – being here in Pennsylvania, Phil Woods’ band was in town you know, and Phil lived in Delaware Water Gap. And his rhythm section guys lived in the Poconos. So I was associated with them. And it’s word of mouth musicians you know. And also in our area I’ll say, Al Cohn – Al Cohn I was at a restaurant playing somewhere and he liked me. So that was the first gig I ever played in New York City was with him at Fat Tuesday’s, a club called Fat Tuesday’s, and we played downstairs. And so that meeting, and this bass player, Phil Woods’ bass player, Steve Gilmore, would recommend me for things you know. And I got to play with Zoot with Al. It was one of Zoot’s last gigs actually, at the Blue Note and I was thrilled to be part of it and we sat in the, I remember sitting in the what do you call it, the green room upstairs at the Blue Note and him complaining about young musicians not knowing tunes, not wanting to know © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
tunes, not learning enough tunes. So that was basically part of our discussion while he hit a little vodka on the side there.
Why would a young musician not find knowing tunes worthwhile?

Well that’s a good question. I did learn them. I mean I did gigs where you had to. It was dance – a lot of times dance music and you’d have to play medleys of tunes. You know Frank Sinatra songbook you know. And I learned to fake as well. So I got away with murder in a lot of ways you know, because I faked. But I mean all the older musicians as I’d say, they all knew those tunes. I mean you had to know those tunes. And I think the younger guys, it’s what they’re listening to. You know they’re listening to Trane, maybe later Trane. Or Miles, the later groups you know. Or the fusion bands of the ‘70s. You know I miss the ‘60s. I was a kid you know, so ‘70s was where I was really starting to play professionally and you know my like for like say fusion music, which I enjoyed, which took me from rock music. I wanted to know how those guys learned what they learned. And so then I heard about Charlie Parker. I heard about Miles Davis. So I went backwards in time, you know, to find out where – you know after the virtuosity you know? A guy that can really kill his instrument. And one of the guys for me of course was New York State’s Scott LaFaro you know. Of course we all – I mean he ruined a lot of bass players I guess for band leaders.
